title: Zoonotic Potential of Influenza A Viruses: A Comprehensive Overview

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Foundational Overview of Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Taxonomy, Host Range, and Cross-Species Emergence
subsections.content:
Influenza A viruses are classified within the family Orthomyxoviridae and are traditionally subtyped by the antigenic properties of hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA). Aquatic wild birds, especially Anseriformes and Charadriiformes, constitute the principal reservoir and harbor extensive HA/NA diversity, including lineages historically identified in shorebirds and terns such as A/tern/South Africa/1961 [ref 4], [ref 5]. This broad avian reservoir underpins the exceptional ecological breadth of influenza A and its recurrent capacity to seed infections in new hosts [ref 3].

Beyond birds, influenza A viruses have established or sporadically infected numerous mammals, including humans, swine, horses, dogs, seals, and whales, illustrating a host range unmatched by most respiratory RNA viruses [ref 3]. Cross-species emergence is driven by repeated spillover from avian reservoirs, adaptation in intermediate or new hosts, and reassortment enabled by the segmented genome; swine are important but not exclusive bridging hosts in this process [ref 3]. Human infection is most often linked to avian-origin viruses such as H5, H7, H9, and H10, with disease severity ranging from conjunctivitis to severe pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome [ref 2], [ref 6].

Recent discoveries expanded influenza A taxonomy and host range further by identifying highly divergent bat-associated lineages in New World bats. H17N10 viruses from Guatemalan bats and H18N11 viruses from Peruvian bats form deeply divergent influenza A lineages, with internal genes that branch outside conventional avian and mammalian diversity and with unusual entry biology suggesting long-standing host-virus association [ref 1], [ref 7]. Although their zoonotic potential remains uncertain, these findings broaden the conceptual landscape of influenza reservoirs and emphasize that cross-species emergence should be viewed through a One Health framework integrating wildlife, domestic animals, and humans [ref 1], [ref 3], [ref 7].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Foundational Overview of Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Historical Evolution and Major Influenza A Outbreaks
subsections.content:
The historical trajectory of influenza A virus (IAV) in humans is defined by the interplay of antigenic drift, reassortment, and episodic zoonotic emergence. Seasonal evolution of human H1N1 and H3N2 viruses reflects continual antigenic change under immune selection, whereas pandemics arise when antigenically novel viruses enter immunologically susceptible populations, often through avian or mixed-origin gene constellations ref [6], ref [6], ref [7].

The 1918 H1N1 pandemic remains the benchmark event, causing extraordinary global mortality and inaugurating the first well-characterized modern influenza pandemic. Reconstruction of the 1918 hemagglutinin showed a virus phylogenetically close to avian lineages yet already mammalian-adapted, consistent with either prior adaptation in humans or an unsampled intermediate evolutionary pathway ref [8], ref [8]. Later pandemics in 1957 (H2N2) and 1968 (H3N2) were classical reassortment events involving acquisition of avian-origin surface glycoprotein genes by previously circulating human viruses ref [6], ref [9], ref [10]. The 1977 re-emergence of H1N1, likely from laboratory release or frozen archival material, was unusual in that it caused a pseudo-pandemic through reintroduction of an older human lineage ref [6], ref [11].

Since the late twentieth century, repeated avian-origin spillovers have underscored persistent pandemic risk. Highly pathogenic H5N1, first recognized in humans in Hong Kong in 1997 and later expanding geographically, demonstrated that severe avian influenza could cross directly into humans with high case fatality but limited sustained transmission ref [5], ref [12], ref [13]. The first recognized human H7N9 infections in China in 2013 further highlighted the threat posed by reassortant avian viruses that circulate silently in poultry yet cause severe human disease ref [9], ref [14]. Together with the 2009 H1N1 pandemic of swine-origin reassortant virus, these events frame IAV history as a continuum of evolution punctuated by major cross-species emergence ref [6], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Foundational Overview of Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Virion Structure, Entry, and Core Replication Features
subsections.content:
Influenza A virions are enveloped, pleomorphic particles whose architecture is organized around a host-derived lipid membrane studded with hemagglutinin (HA), neuraminidase (NA), and the M2 ion channel, with M1 forming an underlying matrix layer and eight segmented vRNPs packaged internally. Quantitative proteomics further indicates that virions reproducibly incorporate selected host proteins and even low levels of NS1, emphasizing that particle composition is structured rather than incidental ref [5].

Entry begins with HA engagement of terminal sialic acids on host glycoconjugates, followed by endocytic uptake. Low endosomal pH then triggers the hallmark HA refolding reaction: after receptor binding at neutral pH, acidification exposes the HA2 fusion peptide and drives a large conformational rearrangement that brings viral and endosomal membranes together for fusion ref [10]. A prerequisite for this step is proteolytic cleavage of the HA0 precursor into HA1 and HA2, which primes HA for fusion competence; viruses with monobasic cleavage sites depend on tissue-restricted extracellular proteases, whereas polybasic H5/H7 cleavage sites allow activation by ubiquitous furin-like proteases and are linked to systemic spread and high pathogenicity ref [6].

Following fusion, M2-mediated acidification promotes uncoating and release of vRNPs, which are imported into the nucleus, an unusual feature among RNA viruses. The viral polymerase transcribes capped viral mRNAs by cap-snatching and replicates the genome through a complementary cRNA intermediate, while NP coats nascent RNAs to form new vRNPs. Assembly occurs at the plasma membrane, where M1 coordinates genome packaging and budding, yielding progeny virions whose morphology and host-derived composition can influence transmission and zoonotic fitness ref [5], ref [10], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Foundational Overview of Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Genome Organization and Canonical Viral Proteins
subsections.content:
Influenza A viruses possess eight negative-sense RNA segments, each packaged as a viral ribonucleoprotein (vRNP) comprising genomic RNA, multiple NP monomers, and a single heterotrimeric polymerase complex of PB2, PB1, and PA. Collectively, these segments encode the canonical structural and non-structural proteins PB2, PB1, PA, HA, NP, NA, M1/M2, and NS1/NEP through a combination of segment-specific transcription, splicing, and alternative coding strategies. Segment 7 yields M1 and the ion channel M2, whereas segment 8 encodes NS1 and, via splicing, NS2/NEP, illustrating how a compact segmented genome maximizes coding output while preserving modular reassortment potential relevant to zoonotic emergence [3], ref [16].

Among the canonical proteins, PB2 mediates cap binding, PB1 contains the polymerase active site, and PA contributes endonuclease activity for cap snatching, while NP encapsidates vRNA and supports transcription and replication. HA and NA form the major surface glycoproteins responsible for attachment/fusion and receptor-destroying activity, respectively, whereas M1 underlies virion morphology and coordinates assembly. M1 also contributes to late-stage vRNP trafficking from the nucleus, supporting the transition from genome replication to particle assembly [1].

The segment-8 products are particularly important for linking genome expression to assembly. NS1 is a multifunctional antagonist of host antiviral responses and also modulates viral RNA synthesis, splicing, and translation [3]. In contrast, NS2/NEP is canonically required for vRNP nuclear export through interactions with cellular export machinery [6], yet it also regulates the balance between transcription and replication, promoting cRNA/vRNA accumulation while reducing mRNA levels in reconstitution systems [4]. Consistent with its structural role in assembly, NS2/NEP associates with virion matrix and binds M1-containing complexes, reinforcing the intimate coupling between genome organization, gene expression, and morphogenesis in influenza A virus [7], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Foundational Overview of Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Accessory Proteins and Expanded Coding Capacity
subsections.content:
Influenza A virus coding capacity extends well beyond the canonical proteins through leaky scanning, alternative splicing, and ribosomal frameshifting. Segment 2 encodes not only PB1 but also PB1-F2 and the N-terminally truncated PB1-N40, illustrating how overlapping reading frames and differential AUG usage expand the proteome ref [22]. Segment 3 similarly produces PA-X through a +1 ribosomal frameshift, a mechanism that links host shutoff activity to polymerase gene expression and is evolutionarily conserved across many influenza A lineages ref [8]. Additional N-terminally truncated PA products, PA-N155 and PA-N182, further underscore that internal initiation within polymerase transcripts is not exceptional but a recurring strategy ref [9].

These accessory products are not uniformly distributed across influenza A evolution, and their retention or truncation can be host-associated. PA-X is broadly conserved, yet truncated X-ORFs have arisen convergently in some mammalian lineages, including swine and canine viruses, suggesting species-specific selective pressures on accessory gene function ref [8]. Likewise, alternative splicing in the NS segment can generate NS3 following an adaptive NS1 mutation linked to host switching; notably, the relevant codon configuration has been associated with avian-to-mammalian emergence events in humans, swine, and dogs ref [13]. Such observations are especially relevant to zoonotic risk because changes in accessory protein expression may accompany or facilitate adaptation in new hosts.

More recently, the PB2 segment was also shown to encode PB2-S1 from a novel spliced mRNA, adding to evidence that even segments long considered monocistronic harbor hidden coding potential ref [14]. Functionally, many of these proteins are dispensable for basic replication in vitro yet can modulate polymerase activity, innate immune antagonism, mitochondrial biology, or virulence ref [22], ref [9], ref [13], ref [14]. Collectively, these findings revise the traditional view of influenza A as a virus with a fixed 10- or 11-protein proteome and instead position it as a genetically economical pathogen whose expanded coding repertoire may influence host range, pathogenesis, and cross-species emergence ref [22], ref [8], ref [9], ref [13], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Evolution, Epidemiology, and Major Zoonotic Influenza A Subtypes
subsections.subsection_title: Evolutionary mechanisms and cross-species emergence of influenza A
subsections.content:
Cross-species emergence of influenza A viruses is driven by the interaction of rapid mutation, genome segmentation, and ecological opportunity at the human–animal interface. Wild aquatic birds remain the major reservoir, but successful host jumps typically require adaptation across multiple barriers, including receptor usage, polymerase function, tissue tropism, and transmission mode ref [3], ref [25]. A One Health perspective is therefore essential, because poultry production systems, live-bird markets, swine husbandry, wildlife movements, and human exposure jointly shape opportunities for spillover and onward adaptation ref [3], ref [25].

A central evolutionary mechanism is reassortment, enabled by the segmented genome when distinct viruses co-infect the same host. Experimental and field studies show that reassortment can occur readily in vivo and repeatedly generates genotypes with altered fitness, host range, and transmissibility ref [24], ref [9]. Ecological context strongly influences this process: avian influenza viruses circulating in wild birds evolve more slowly than poultry-adapted lineages, consistent with differences in transmission routes, host density, and selection pressures ref [23]. Once established in poultry, H5 viruses have undergone extensive diversification, with panzootic expansion fueled by reassortment and local adaptation rather than repeated de novo emergence from wild birds ref [26], ref [10].

These dynamics help explain why certain subtypes repeatedly seed zoonotic infections. Poultry and swine act as epidemiologic amplifiers and genetic interfaces where avian, mammalian, and human-adapted traits can be combined, while genomics increasingly resolves the timing and direction of such events ref [25], ref [10]. Recent examples, including H5N1 viruses acquiring an H9N2-derived PB1 gene in Bangladeshi poultry, illustrate how endemic low-pathogenic lineages can donate internal genes that may reshape replication or host adaptation potential ref [9]. Thus, zoonotic emergence is best understood not as a single mutation event, but as a multistep eco-evolutionary process operating across connected host populations ref [3], ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Evolution, Epidemiology, and Major Zoonotic Influenza A Subtypes
subsections.subsection_title: Global epidemiology and diversification of highly pathogenic H5 viruses
subsections.content:
Highly pathogenic H5 viruses of the A/goose/Guangdong/1/1996 lineage have transformed avian influenza from largely localized poultry epizootics into a prolonged transcontinental panzootic. Successive waves of H5N1 expansion across Asia, Europe, Africa, and parts of North America were accompanied by persistent diversification of the HA gene, necessitating repeated updates to clade nomenclature and underscoring geographically structured evolution in enzootic poultry systems ref [30], ref [3]. Early dissemination was followed by establishment of regionally distinct lineages, including repeated introductions into South Asia; Bangladesh, for example, experienced multiple incursions of H5N1, initially dominated by clade 2.2.2 and later replaced by clade 2.3.2.1 viruses circulating in live bird markets ref [4].

A major epidemiologic shift occurred with the emergence of clade 2.3.4.4 H5Nx viruses, whose broad host range and compatibility with diverse neuraminidase and internal-gene constellations facilitated rapid global spread. Clade 2.3.4.4 H5N8 disseminated intercontinentally through migratory flyways in 2014–2015 and again in reassorted forms thereafter, while local reassortment with Eurasian and North American avian influenza viruses generated H5N2, H5N5, and additional H5N8 variants ref [30], ref [5], ref [6]. This diversification blurred the boundary between wild-bird-mediated long-distance spread and poultry-maintained endemicity, with domestic ducks and live poultry markets serving as major amplification interfaces ref [30], ref [5].

Among clade 2.3.4.4 descendants, H5N6 became especially important because it combined broad poultry circulation with recurrent human infection. Phylogenetic analyses indicate that H5N6 arose through at least two independent reassortment pathways involving clade 2.3.4.4 H5 viruses and N6 genes from H6N6 viruses, followed by further exchange of internal genes with clade 2.3.2.1c H5N1 and, later, H9N2 viruses ref [5]. Multiple reassortant H5N6 genotypes subsequently spread across southern China and into Laos and Vietnam, with some lineages showing mammalian-adaptive markers and antigenic divergence relevant to zoonotic risk ref [5], ref [7]. Overall, the global epidemiology of highly pathogenic H5 viruses is therefore best understood as recurrent clade replacement layered upon continual reassortment, ecological expansion, and long-distance dispersal ref [30], ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Evolution, Epidemiology, and Major Zoonotic Influenza A Subtypes
subsections.subsection_title: H7 subtype emergence and human infection dynamics
subsections.content:
H7 viruses have shown a distinctive zoonotic profile among avian influenza A subtypes. Before the emergence of H7N9, documented human H7 infections were linked to H7N7, H7N3, and H7N2 outbreaks in Europe and North America and were typically characterized by conjunctivitis or mild influenza-like illness, although severe pneumonia and one fatal case occurred during the 2003 Netherlands H7N7 epidemic [2][4]. The British Columbia H7N3 outbreak further illustrated that occupational poultry exposure, especially with breaches in eye protection, can be sufficient for transmission, while secondary spread remained limited [2].

The epidemiologic landscape changed markedly in 2013 when H7N9 was recognized in humans in eastern China [1]. Genetic analyses showed that the zoonotic H7N9 lineage arose through reassortment involving H7 and N9 viruses ultimately derived from domestic duck and wild-bird gene pools, with internal genes donated by enzootic poultry H9N2 viruses [3]. Live poultry markets were identified as the immediate interface for spillover, and market closures were temporally associated with declines in human cases, underscoring the importance of silent circulation in chickens and market amplification [1][3].

Clinically, H7N9 differed from earlier H7 infections by causing a high proportion of severe viral pneumonia and ARDS, particularly in older adults with comorbidities, while still lacking evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission [4]. The later emergence of highly pathogenic H7N9 variants in Guangdong signaled further adaptation within poultry: these viruses acquired a polybasic HA cleavage site, spread geographically, and in some patients also harbored neuraminidase inhibitor resistance mutations such as R292K, compounding treatment concerns [5][6]. Together, H7 viruses exemplify how repeated avian-to-human introductions can range from mild ocular disease to severe respiratory infection, depending on subtype, genotype, and the ecology of poultry exposure [4][5][6].

subsections.section_title: Evolution, Epidemiology, and Major Zoonotic Influenza A Subtypes
subsections.subsection_title: H9N2 as a widespread zoonotic reservoir and gene donor
subsections.content:
H9N2 influenza viruses have become one of the most pervasive avian influenza lineages in poultry and a recurrent source of zoonotic exposure. Early human infections in Hong Kong and southern China established that direct avian-to-human transmission can occur, usually causing mild disease that is likely to be underdetected in routine surveillance [1]. Virologic analyses further showed that some human H9N2 isolates were closely related to quail- and poultry-derived viruses and shared a distinctive internal-gene constellation with the 1997 H5N1 viruses, immediately raising concern that H9N2 lineages possess unusual compatibility with human infection [1, 2].

A central reason H9N2 is regarded as a major zoonotic reservoir is its progressive adaptation in poultry together with molecular traits favoring mammalian entry. Poultry H9N2 viruses circulating in Asia were shown to display human virus-like receptor specificity, particularly linked to HA features such as Leu226, and accompanying changes in neuraminidase consistent with adaptation outside wild-bird reservoirs [3]. In China, long-term endemic circulation, extensive diversification, and the dominance of genotypes with enhanced fitness in chickens have created a large and dynamic gene pool from which other zoonotic reassortants can emerge [5]. Indeed, H9N2 has repeatedly acted as a donor of internal genes not only to H5N1 in Hong Kong but later to other avian-origin human threats, underscoring its role as a reassortment backbone rather than merely a spillover virus [2, 5].

Epidemiologically, H9N2 now spans much of Asia and is also deeply established across the Middle East and North Africa, where multiple G1-like phylogroups, panzootic lineages, frequent co-infections, and occasional mammalian infections indicate sustained opportunities for adaptation and regional spread [4]. Human disease remains sporadic, but serology reveals far broader exposure than case counts suggest: among occupationally exposed populations in China, H9N2 seropositivity was highest in live-poultry-market and farming workers and was greater in southern than northern provinces [6]. Together, these data support viewing H9N2 as a widespread zoonotic reservoir whose greatest public-health importance lies in its dual capacity for repeated subclinical human infection and for donating internal genes to emergent influenza A viruses [4–6].

subsections.section_title: Evolution, Epidemiology, and Major Zoonotic Influenza A Subtypes
subsections.subsection_title: Other emerging zoonotic subtypes and mammalian spillover
subsections.content:
Beyond H5, H7, and H9N2, several low-pathogenic avian influenza lineages have demonstrated repeated capacity for mammalian infection and occasional human disease. H10 viruses are particularly notable: the human-infecting H10N8 virus detected in China arose through reassortment, with H10 and N8 surface genes tracing to wild-bird lineages and multiple internal genes derived from poultry H9N2 viruses, underscoring the continuing role of live-poultry systems in generating zoonotic constellations ref [42].

Experimental data further indicate that other ostensibly low-pathogenic avian subtypes merit surveillance. Diverse H6 viruses productively infect mice and ferrets without prior adaptation and can cause respiratory illness, showing that broad circulation in birds can coexist with appreciable mammalian tropism ref [43]. Such findings are consistent with the view that subtype alone is a poor predictor of zoonotic risk.

Mammalian spillover has also been documented in marine mammals. During the 2014–2015 northwestern European harbor seal die-off, avian-origin H10N7 was associated with mass mortality and respiratory tract infection, with viral antigen largely confined to airway epithelium and fatal outcomes often compounded by secondary bacterial pneumonia ref [46], ref [45]. The same seal H10N7 virus replicated in experimentally infected ferrets, causing mild-to-moderate respiratory disease and supporting concern for zoonotic potential ref [45]. Follow-up reverse-genetics work showed that seal-associated HA substitutions, especially Q220L, increased affinity for mammalian-type receptors while retaining efficient replication in avian cells, illustrating how limited adaptive change may facilitate cross-species emergence without full host specialization ref [6]. Collectively, these events show that multiple non-H5/H7 subtypes can breach mammalian barriers and should be incorporated into One Health surveillance at the wildlife–poultry–human interface ref [46], ref [42], ref [43].

subsections.section_title: Sources and Molecular Determinants of Zoonotic Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: Ecological and Epidemiologic Sources of Human Exposure
subsections.content:
Human exposure to zoonotic influenza A viruses is structured by a small number of recurrent ecological interfaces: backyard or household poultry keeping, live-bird marketing and slaughter, occupational contact with swine, and selected wildlife-associated activities. Across H5N1-endemic regions, a One Health perspective has emphasized that risk is not determined solely by virus circulation in animals, but by the coupling of poultry production systems, trade networks, consumer preference for live birds, household husbandry, and limited biosecurity in small-scale settings ref [47]. In the Greater Mekong sub-region and Bangladesh, dense live-poultry trading systems and repeated viral introductions into poultry create sustained opportunities for human exposure, especially where birds from multiple sources are mixed and handled ref [47], ref [12].

For avian-origin infections, the strongest epidemiologic signal remains direct or proximate contact with infected poultry. A systematic review of H5N1 identified slaughtering, defeathering, food preparation, handling sick or dead birds, exposure in live-bird markets, and contact with contaminated water or fomites as the dominant pathways at the animal-human interface ref [51]. Country experience reinforces this pattern: in Egypt, human infection clustered around the Nile Delta, where backyard flocks, live-bird markets, and mixed waterfowl-chicken systems sustained extensive circulation despite control efforts ref [50]. In China, H7N9 emerged from poultry-market networks seeded by avian viruses whose progenitors moved from domestic ducks into chickens and reassorted with endemic H9N2 viruses, highlighting live-bird markets as both exposure sites and evolutionary incubators ref [13]. Fatality patterns also differ by subtype, but older age, comorbidity, and delayed diagnosis amplify risk once infection occurs ref [11].

Swine-associated exposure represents a distinct zoonotic pathway. Serologic data from the United Kingdom showed elevated A(H1N1)pdm09 infection risk among pig industry workers relative to a community comparison cohort, consistent with bidirectional transmission at the human-swine interface and the role of pigs as occupationally relevant mixing hosts ref [32]. By contrast, wildlife-associated exposure appears more episodic and interface-specific: among California-exposed groups, waterfowl hunters had substantially higher contact risk with avian-influenza-positive wildlife than casual or occupational wildlife contacts ref [9]. Overall, these studies indicate that zoonotic emergence is most likely where high viral prevalence, repeated animal mixing, and intense human handling coincide—particularly in live-bird markets, household poultry systems, and pig production networks ref [51], ref [32], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Sources and Molecular Determinants of Zoonotic Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: Polymerase and Internal Gene Determinants of Mammalian Adaptation
subsections.content:
Among viral factors that shape zoonotic potential, the polymerase complex and other internal genes are central determinants of whether an avian influenza A virus can replicate efficiently in mammalian cells. Classical host-range studies identified PB2, PB1, PA, NP, M, and NS as major contributors to species specificity, with polymerase activity often emerging as the dominant bottleneck after cross-species transmission ref [54]. In particular, PB2 residue 627 is a canonical mammalian-adaptive marker: avian viruses typically encode 627E, whereas 627K enhances replication at lower temperatures characteristic of the mammalian upper airway and reduces the cold sensitivity of avian polymerases ref [58]. In vivo, mammalian transmission is also promoted by PB2 627K or compensatory constellations such as 627E/701N, illustrating that alternative adaptive routes can converge on improved polymerase function in mammals ref [60].

Adaptation is not restricted to PB2-627 alone. Other PB2 changes, including 271A together with the 590/591 SR polymorphism, can substantially increase replication and virulence in swine-origin backgrounds, highlighting the importance of epistatic compensation within polymerase subunits ref [55]. Pandemic history further underscores the role of internal genes: the 1957 H2N2 and 1968 H3N2 viruses acquired avian-origin PB1 segments, and experimental reconstruction indicates that the avian PB1 gene facilitated replication and transmissibility of the 1968 pandemic virus in mammals ref [9], ref [12]. Likewise, the PA segment can mediate species jumps, as reassortment and adaptive mutation in PA have been shown to help avian polymerases overcome mammalian restrictions ref [18].

Beyond the polymerase trimer, other internal segments modulate mammalian adaptation by altering replication efficiency, cell tropism, and immune antagonism. The NS segment is a notable example: transfer of the NS gene from an H5N1 highly pathogenic avian virus was sufficient to change the host range properties of an H7N1 virus, emphasizing that successful emergence can depend on cooperative effects among polymerase and non-polymerase internal genes ref [20]. Together, these findings support a constellation model of adaptation in which zoonotic risk is amplified not by single mutations alone, but by compatible internal-gene combinations that stabilize polymerase activity and counter host-specific barriers ref [54], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Sources and Molecular Determinants of Zoonotic Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: Host Restriction, Nuclear Import, and Innate Immune Barriers
subsections.content:
Host restriction at the mammalian species barrier is shaped not only by polymerase catalytic efficiency, but also by the ability of incoming vRNPs to access the nucleus and evade innate restriction. Classical import studies established that influenza vRNA is not imported autonomously; rather, NP provides the effective nuclear localization signal and uses the canonical import pathway with importin-α/β, Ran and p10 to deliver vRNPs into the nucleus ref [9]. Subsequent work showed that host range is influenced by selective engagement of importin-α isoforms by PB2 and NP, with altered PB2/NP-importin interactions modulating cell tropism and adaptation to mammalian cells ref [13], ref [14], ref [15].

These trafficking requirements intersect directly with intrinsic immunity. Human MxA restricts influenza A virus at an early post-entry step by retaining incoming genomes in the cytoplasm and blocking efficient nuclear access, identifying vRNP import itself as a key zoonotic bottleneck ref [61]. Sensitivity to MxA is determined largely by NP, and avian viruses are generally more susceptible than human-adapted strains ref [64]. Pandemic lineages escaped this barrier through adaptive, surface-exposed NP mutations that reduce MxA restriction, although such escape can impose fitness trade-offs in avian backgrounds ref [65]. Thus, successful zoonotic emergence requires compatibility with both nuclear import machinery and human intrinsic restriction factors.

Innate immune evasion after entry further conditions replication in humans. NS1 is the major multifunctional antagonist of interferon induction and effector pathways, acting through inhibition of RIG-I signaling, PKR activation, host mRNA processing/export, and selective support of viral gene expression ref [16]. Variation in NS1 sequence and binding interfaces can therefore modulate how efficiently newly introduced avian-origin viruses suppress human antiviral responses. Together, nuclear import usage, MxA escape, and NS1-mediated antagonism form a linked set of barriers that strongly influence whether spillover infection remains abortive or progresses toward sustained mammalian adaptation ref [61], ref [65], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Sources and Molecular Determinants of Zoonotic Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: Surface Glycoproteins and Receptor Determinants of Cross-Species Transmission
subsections.content:
Cross-species transmission of influenza A virus is initiated by the surface glycoproteins, especially hemagglutinin (HA), which mediates attachment to terminal sialylated glycans and low-pH membrane fusion; thus, changes in HA receptor recognition are central to zoonotic adaptation ref [70]. A canonical host-range distinction is the preference of most avian viruses for α2,3-linked sialic acids and of human-adapted viruses for α2,6-linked receptors, but this binary view is incomplete because receptor topology, density, and tissue context strongly shape productive binding and entry ref [70], ref [74], ref [54].

Receptor availability differs markedly among hosts and tissues. In humans, α2,6-linked glycans predominate in much of the upper respiratory tract, whereas α2,3-linked structures are enriched in bronchioles, alveoli, and some ocular tissues, helping explain why many avian viruses infect humans sporadically yet transmit poorly ref [74]. In addition, the chemical species of sialic acid matters: Neu5Gc is abundant in several mammals but essentially absent in humans, and recognition of Neu5Gc-containing α2,3 glycans can therefore constrain or redirect host range ref [73].

Specific HA substitutions can shift receptor usage toward human airway targets, but this usually requires coordinated, often multistep change. For H5 HA, combinations of receptor-binding site mutations were shown to confer binding to human tracheal epithelium, whereas intermediate genotypes often remained poorly adapted, highlighting a substantial genetic barrier to emergence ref [9]. Complementary computational and experimental work likewise identified H5 residues that enhance human receptor specificity, and studies of pandemic H1N1 showed that HA position 222 modulates receptor binding and tropism rather than simply increasing affinity in a uniform way ref [19], ref [15]. Surface adaptation is also constrained by the need to preserve HA-NA functional balance, because reduced receptor avidity or altered neuraminidase cleavage can compensate for one another, and efficient replication depends on this coevolved equilibrium ref [20].

subsections.section_title: Sources and Molecular Determinants of Zoonotic Transmission
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic Diversity, Reassortment, and Experimental Systems Informing Emergence
subsections.content:
Genetic diversity and reassortment are central to influenza A virus emergence because segmented genomes permit rapid assembly of novel constellations with altered host range, fitness, and immune evasion. Field surveillance repeatedly shows that zoonotic-risk lineages such as H9N2 are not genetically static: Egyptian pigeon H9N2 isolates acquired five internal genes from Eurasian avian viruses, while quail-associated H9N2 viruses displayed antigenic drift, underscoring how mixed avian ecologies can generate both genotypic and phenotypic novelty relevant to human exposure and adaptation [3]. Similar principles underlie past pandemic emergence, in which avian-origin internal genes, including PB1, contributed to the 1957 and 1968 human pandemic viruses, highlighting reassortment as a recurrent route for zoonotic transition.

Experimental reassortment studies further show that individual internal segments can substantially reshape replication and host responses after cross-lineage exchange. NS-segment swapping can alter viral RNA synthesis, innate immune antagonism, cell tropism, and overall propagation in a strain- and host-dependent manner, including in highly pathogenic H7 backgrounds and in H1N1pdm09 viruses carrying a 1918-descended PR8 NS segment [11, 17]. More broadly, in vivo reassortment experiments demonstrate that mixed infection can generate transmissible mammalian-adapted progeny, emphasizing that emergence risk reflects compatibility among whole gene constellations rather than single mutations alone.

Reverse-genetics systems have been indispensable for dissecting these processes. The recovery of influenza A virus entirely from cloned cDNAs established a platform to build defined reassortants and test causal links between genotype and phenotype [5]. Subsequent improvements that overcome instability of volatile HA inserts, including low-copy vectors and alternative bacterial hosts, have made rescue of otherwise difficult avian H5 and H9 genomes more reliable, thereby accelerating studies of emergence, vaccine seed generation, and risk assessment [1]. Together with animal, organ culture, and cell-based systems, these tools provide a mechanistic bridge from surveillance-detected diversity to experimentally validated zoonotic potential.

subsections.section_title: Prevention and Therapeutic Strategies Against Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Vaccine Development and Reverse-Genetics Platforms
subsections.content:
Reverse-genetics platforms have transformed influenza A vaccine development by enabling rapid, sequence-defined rescue of candidate vaccine viruses directly from cloned cDNAs, thereby avoiding the slow and stochastic selection of classical reassortants. Foundational plasmid-based systems first demonstrated recovery of influenza A virus entirely from cloned cDNAs and were soon adapted to plasmid-only rescue of 6 + 2 vaccine candidates carrying contemporary HA and NA genes on a PR8 internal-gene backbone, providing a practical framework for seasonal and prepandemic vaccine seed generation [3, ref 4, ref 5].

This approach was particularly important for zoonotic avian strains with poor growth or high pathogenicity. A landmark example was the reverse-genetics-derived H5N1 vaccine candidate in which the multibasic HA cleavage site was removed while preserving antigenicity; the resulting H5N1/PR8 reassortant was attenuated in chickens and mice, remained immunogenic, and protected mice against wild-type H5N1 challenge [2]. Such rational engineering illustrates how reverse genetics improves biosafety while retaining relevant surface antigens for pandemic preparedness [2, ref 6].

Platform optimization has also focused on manufacturing compatibility. In Vero cells, substitution of the PR8 NS segment with that of a Vero-adapted reassortant improved rescue efficiency and accelerated growth of multiple subtype combinations, including H1N1, H3N2, H6N1, and H9N2, without detectable HA antigenic change [1]. Together, plasmid-only rescue, high-growth PR8-based backbones, and cell-culture-adapted master strains have established reverse genetics as the core enabling technology for scalable influenza vaccine seed production against both human and zoonotic influenza A threats [1, 3, ref 4].

subsections.section_title: Prevention and Therapeutic Strategies Against Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Vaccine Efficacy and Cross-Protection in Animal and Field Settings
subsections.content:
Vaccine performance against influenza A viruses in animal populations is best judged not only by survival after challenge, but also by reduction of replication, shedding, and onward transmission. In poultry, this distinction is critical because partial protection can mask infection while sustaining enzootic circulation. In Egypt, cross-reactivity studies under field-like conditions showed that most commercial H5 vaccines generated weak antibody responses against contemporary H5N1 strains, whereas a vaccine based on an Egyptian H5N1 isolate induced substantially higher homologous and cross-reactive titres, underscoring the importance of antigenic matching and local strain updating ref [85]. Similar conclusions emerged when commercial H5 products were tested against newly emerged Egyptian H5N8 viruses: some vaccines limited mortality, but only a homologous experimental H5N8 vaccine and selected matched products markedly suppressed shedding, indicating that clinical protection alone overestimates field utility ref [84].

Field studies reinforce these laboratory findings. In Indonesian commercial layers, long-term follow-up of vaccinated flocks revealed highly variable flock-level immunity, frequent waning of protective HI titres, and inconsistent responses across farms and vaccination schedules; only a minority of intensively revaccinated flocks maintained protection late in lay, highlighting the operational fragility of vaccine programs under real production conditions ref [5]. More broadly, field and modeling analyses from endemic settings show that vaccination can reduce outbreak incidence and transmission, but only when coupled to surveillance, antigenic updating, and adequate coverage ref [5]. These observations help explain how suboptimal vaccination may facilitate silent infection and potential antigenic escape rather than durable control ref [85].

Comparable principles apply in swine, where cross-protection is constrained by rapid antigenic drift and maternal antibody interference. Commercial US swine H3 vaccines showed variable serologic cross-reactivity to contemporary H3N2 strains, with reduced coverage against emerging H3N2v-like viruses; the best-matched product decreased lung replication and nasal shedding in pigs without maternal antibodies, but protection was blunted when maternal antibodies were present ref [86]. In direct comparative studies, both inactivated and live attenuated vaccines reduced disease after H3N2v-like challenge, yet live attenuated vaccination more effectively blocked nasal shedding and indirect transmission, despite lower serum HI titres, indicating that mucosal immunity may better predict interruption of zoonotic-risk interfaces than serum serology alone ref [87]. Together, animal and field data argue that vaccine efficacy should be defined by prevention of transmission as much as prevention of death ref [84], ref [87].

subsections.section_title: Prevention and Therapeutic Strategies Against Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Alternative and Broad Prevention Strategies in Avian Influenza Control
subsections.content:
Beyond strain-matched vaccination, avian influenza control in poultry relies on layered, broad-spectrum measures that reduce exposure pressure and viral amplification across production systems. Reviews of H5N1 control emphasize that surveillance, movement control, market hygiene, stamping-out, and especially enforceable farm biosecurity remain foundational, because vaccination alone may not prevent infection, shedding, or silent circulation in endemic settings ref [89]. Field observations from Egypt further underscore this point: H5N1 was detected across commercial farms, live-bird markets, abattoirs, backyard sectors, and even wild egrets, indicating that prevention must target the entire poultry value chain rather than individual flocks alone ref [4].

Alternative interventions proposed for poultry include antiviral chemotherapy, natural products, probiotics, innate immune stimulants, RNA interference, and host-genetic approaches ref [89]. However, use of adamantanes in poultry is strongly discouraged because rapid selection and transmission of resistant variants can compromise drugs critical for human medicine; neuraminidase inhibitors may reduce transmission experimentally but are costly and impractical for routine flock-level use ref [89]. Herbal compounds and probiotics have shown antiviral or immunomodulatory activity against H5 or H9 viruses in experimental systems, but evidence is heterogeneous and standardization, field efficacy, and residue or safety issues remain unresolved ref [89].

More forward-looking broad prevention strategies aim to make poultry intrinsically less permissive to infection. These include chicken interferon or Toll-like receptor agonists to transiently enhance innate defenses, siRNA platforms directed at conserved viral genes, and selective breeding or transgenic approaches exploiting host resistance loci such as Mx or duck-like RIG-I pathways ref [89]. Such tools are attractive because they are less dependent on antigenic matching and may retain activity despite viral drift ref [89]. Still, delivery, cost, regulatory acceptance, durability, and scalability remain major barriers, so current evidence supports their role as complementary—not replacement—measures within integrated One Health control programs for endemic avian influenza ref [89], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Prevention and Therapeutic Strategies Against Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Antiviral Drugs Targeting Viral Proteins and Resistance Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Direct-acting anti-influenza drugs have mainly targeted the M2 ion channel, neuraminidase (NA), and, more recently, hemagglutinin-mediated membrane fusion. The adamantanes amantadine and rimantadine inhibit M2-dependent uncoating, but their utility has been severely undermined by the rapid selection and global dissemination of resistance-associated M2 substitutions, especially S31N, which now predominates in many influenza A lineages ref [91], ref [92], ref [93]. This historical experience illustrates a central principle in influenza therapeutics: viral protein targets with low genetic barriers or minimal fitness cost for escape can quickly lose clinical value.

NA inhibitors remain the best-established class for both seasonal and zoonotic influenza A management. Zanamivir and oseltamivir act by blocking sialic-acid cleavage and virion release, and their mechanism is tightly linked to the structural organization of the NA active site ref [90], ref [94]. However, resistance can emerge through catalytic-site or framework mutations that reduce drug binding while preserving sufficient enzymatic function. Epidemiologic and clinical analyses have shown that resistance patterns differ by subtype and antiviral pressure, requiring continuous phenotypic and sequence-based surveillance ref [92], ref [94]. In zoonotic strains, this issue is especially important because NA inhibitor susceptibility cannot be assumed across avian-origin viruses.

Recent examples emphasize that resistance is shaped not only by primary escape mutations but also by compensatory evolution. Oseltamivir-resistant A(H7N9) viruses have acquired NA substitutions that diminish susceptibility, while in A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses permissive NA changes can offset fitness costs and facilitate onward circulation of resistant variants ref [97], ref [9]. Beyond NA, fusion inhibitors such as arbidol target the HA conformational transition required for endosomal membrane fusion, expanding the antiviral repertoire against influenza A ref [11]. Overall, resistance management in zoonotic influenza requires subtype-specific susceptibility testing, combination or sequential treatment strategies where appropriate, and genomic surveillance to detect resistant variants before they become entrenched in animal reservoirs or spill over into humans ref [92], ref [93], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Prevention and Therapeutic Strategies Against Influenza A Viruses
subsections.subsection_title: Host-Directed and Nucleic Acid-Based Antiviral Therapies
subsections.content:
Host-directed antiviral strategies aim to suppress influenza A virus (IAV) replication by targeting cellular pathways co-opted by the virus, thereby increasing the genetic barrier to resistance. Two of the most developed host targets are NF-κB and Raf/MEK/ERK signaling, both of which facilitate late-stage viral ribonucleoprotein export and productive replication. Inhaled lysine-acetylsalicylate glycine (LASAG; BAY 81-8781), an NF-κB inhibitor, showed broad in vitro activity against human and avian IAVs and reduced lung titers in mice, while aerosolized administration improved symptom alleviation in hospitalized patients with severe influenza in a phase II proof-of-concept trial ref [99], ref [102]. Mechanistically, LASAG suppresses NF-κB-dependent proviral signaling and can also attenuate inflammatory cytokine induction, an attractive feature in severe disease ref [99], ref [102].

The Raf/MEK/ERK axis has likewise emerged as a robust host dependency pathway. The MEK inhibitor CI-1040 inhibited diverse influenza A strains, including highly pathogenic avian viruses and an oseltamivir-resistant H275Y variant, and in mice retained efficacy when treatment was delayed up to 48 h post-infection, exceeding the window observed for standard oseltamivir therapy ref [100]. Trametinib, a clinically approved MEK inhibitor, similarly blocked replication of multiple IAV subtypes in vitro and in vivo by retaining progeny vRNPs in the nucleus, while also reducing expression of IL-6, CCL5, and CXCL10, suggesting dual antiviral and immunomodulatory effects ref [101]. These findings support drug repurposing of oncology kinase inhibitors as adjuncts or combination partners for influenza treatment ref [100], ref [101].

Nucleic acid-based approaches provide a complementary route to suppress viral gene expression directly at the RNA level. Radavirsen (AVI-7100), a PMOplus antisense oligonucleotide targeting the highly conserved M segment and blocking M1/M2 translation and splicing, was safe and well tolerated in a phase I study; exposure at 8 mg/kg achieved plasma AUC values considered therapeutically relevant based on ferret protection studies ref [98]. Earlier morpholino and RNA interference studies also demonstrated reduced lung titers and improved survival in mouse models, supporting the feasibility of sequence-guided antivirals against conserved influenza transcripts ref [98]. Overall, host-directed and nucleic acid-based therapies remain especially attractive for zoonotic and emerging IAVs because they may retain activity despite antigenic drift and classical antiviral resistance, although optimization of delivery, safety, and clinical efficacy remains essential ref [98], ref [99], ref [101].

subsections.section_title: Concluding and Back Matter Elements
subsections.subsection_title: Concluding and Back Matter Elements
subsections.content:
In conclusion, the zoonotic potential of influenza A viruses is best understood as an emergent property of viral evolution at the animal–human interface, shaped by reassortment, mutational adaptation, receptor compatibility, host innate restriction, and ecological opportunity rather than by any single molecular marker alone ref [53], ref [59], ref [3], ref [25]. Repeated spillover events involving H5, H7, H9, and other avian-origin viruses, together with occasional transmission from swine and wildlife reservoirs, demonstrate that pandemic risk is distributed across a broad and dynamic viral landscape ref [2], ref [52], ref [33], ref [103].

A central lesson from the literature is that surveillance must integrate genomics, phenotypic characterization, and exposure-context data across poultry, swine, wild birds, mammals, and humans within a One Health framework ref [28], ref [51], ref [49]. Priorities for future work include improved risk assessment of emerging reassortants, clearer interpretation of seroepidemiologic evidence, routine evaluation of mammalian-adaptive signatures in their genetic background, and better linkage of animal outbreak intelligence to clinical preparedness, diagnostics, vaccines, and antiviral policy ref [41], ref [26].

Back matter for a survey of this scope should therefore emphasize transparent reporting of search strategy, reference selection, nomenclature, and limitations, while highlighting unresolved questions on host range prediction, intermediate hosts, and the determinants of sustained human transmission ref [3], ref [28], ref [49], ref [6]. Such synthesis is essential not only for summarizing current knowledge but also for guiding interdisciplinary preparedness against the next influenza A zoonosis.
